L44@P1: 1. Introduction
L45@P1: In the 90’s the logician R. Laver [11], [12], motivated by questions in the theory
L46@P1: of large cardinals, introduced the so-called Laver tables, which are the subject of
L47@P1: this paper. In short, a Laver table is a finite set endowed with a binary operation
L48@P1: ?, which is left distributive, meaning that p ? (q ? r) = (p ? q) ? (p ? r) holds for all
L49@P1: p, q, r, and in which one of the elements acts, by right multiplication, as a cyclic
L50@P1: permutation of the elements of the set. The formal definition is given in section 2
L51@P1: below. Laver established the existence and uniqueness of such a structure for sets
L52@P1: of cardinal 2n, for some integer n, moreover he discovered many of their interesting
L53@P1: combinatorial properties. Some further work was done at that time, mainly by
L54@P1: logicians and algebraists, notably Dehornoy, Dougherty, Dr´apal, Jech, however it
L55@P1: seems that this subject has been largely ignored by combinatorialists despite the
L56@P1: fact that the Laver tables have a strong and highly nontrivial combinatorial content.
L57@P1: In this paper I will present some of the most basic properties of Laver tables, from a
L58@P1: combinatorial perspective, but I will also try to give some indications on the notions
L59@P1: of set theory which lead to their discovery. I hope that this paper might encourage
L60@P1: combinatorialists to look deeper into this beautiful subject. As I mentioned above,
L61@P1: the Laver tables carry a left distributive operation. The study of such operations
L62@P1: is not part of the mainstream of algebraic combinatorics rather, it comes from two
L63@P1: other sources, set theory and the theory of braids. A lot of information about these
L64@P1: subjects may be found in P. Dehornoy’s book [1] or his recent preprint [3]. The
L65@P1: difficulty in studying left distributive structures comes from the fact that the left
L66@P1: distributive identity p ? (q ? r) = (p ? q) ? (p ? r) does not have the same number
L67@P1: of terms on each side. This implies that computing with operations satisfying this
L68@P1: identity leads to deep recursions. On the other hand experimental study of the
L69@P1: Laver tables, which can be made, up to rather large size, using computers, shows
L70@P1: that these tables seem both to satisfy many regularity properties and yet to escape
L71@P1: any global description. In particular some basic questions have surprising answers:
L72@P1: Laver has proved, using a large cardinal axiom, which is not provable in usual
L73@P1: ZFC theory, that the projective limit of the Laver tables is a free system. As we
L74@P1: shall see below this statement has a very concrete translation into properties of the
L75@P1: Laver tables: it asserts that a certain sequence, with an elementary combinatorial
L76@P1: definition, is unbounded. However, up to now no proof is known of this fact which
L77@P1: does not use this large cardinal axiom. It is a challenge for combinatorialists to
L78@P1: find an elementary proof of this fact (or to disprove it...). This situation bears
L79@P1: some resemblance with the study of the iteration of rational maps on the complex
L80@P1: plane in complex dynamics, which gives rise to Julia sets or the Mandelbrot set (see
L81@P1: e.g. [14]): these objects also are constructed by very simple recursive laws, they
L82@P1: exhibit some regularity and beautiful features, which can be seen on the computer
L83@P1: generated pictures that are easily found on the internet, yet their structure is very
L84@P1: complicated and many questions concerning them are still open. I hope that Laver
L85@P1: tables might attract similar attention from the combinatorialists which would lead
L86@P1-2: to much progress.LAVER 3
L87@P2: This paper is organized as follows: in the next section we give the definition
L88@P2: of Laver tables and make some general comments on left-distributive operations.
L89@P2: In section 3 we give some basic properties of Laver tables then, in section 4, we
L90@P2: explain how these objects were discovered by Laver, starting from considerations
L91@P2: of set theory. We go on with some further properties of Laver tables in sections 5
L92@P2: and 6. We explain in section 7 why these are interesting and subtle combinatorial
L93@P2: objects. In particular we state some difficult open problems. In section 8, we
L94@P2: show that the periods of Laver tables have asymptotic frequencies, which define a
L95@P2: probability measure on N∪ {∞}. It would be interesting to describe more precisely
L96@P2: this probability distribution. Finally, in section 9, we introduce a particular class of
L97@P2: elements of the Laver tables. These are, in some sense, the simplest elements and
L98@P2: a remarkable property of these elements is that they form a subset which is stable
L99@P2: under the operation of the Laver table. Moreover they are parameterized by binary
L100@P2: partitions which are objects related to more mainstream algebraic combinatorics.
L101@P2: Most of the results of this paper are not new, except perhaps the content of section 8
L102@P2: and 9, and can be found in the papers cited in the bibliography, although sometimes
L103@P2: in slightly different form, so that I did not try to track down the exact reference
L104@P2: for each of them.
L105@P2: I would like to thank Patrick Dehornoy for introducing me to this beautiful
L106@P2: subject, as well as Ales Dr´apal for communicating me his preprint [10]. Both of
L107@P2: them made useful remarks on a first version of this paper.
